To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) D-ETGs are more likely to be disturbed than control ETGs, suggesting that they are merger remnants, (ii) D-ETG environments are less dense than the general ETG environment, consistent with a merger origin, (iii) D-ETGS are bluer and more likely to be active than control ETGs and (iv) the dust content of D-ETGS is consistent with an external origin and is not related to the triggered star formation.

the dust and molecular gas content of a sample of 352 nearby ETGs with prominent dust lanes (‘dusty ETGs’, or D-ETGs)
the properties of the dust and associated molecular content in D-ETGs, and we find that the dust content is consistent with the accretion of gas-rich dwarfs in minor mergers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dust and molecular gas content of these ETGs is consistent with a minor dry merger origin, with a gas fraction in the progenitors of 20–44 per cent.
the dust in D-ETGs originates in gas-rich dwarf satellites that have merged into their host ETGs.
D-ETGs are a mixed bag: some are likely to be formed by major mergers, some by minor mergers with gas-rich satellites, some by major mergers with gas-poor satellites, and some by minor dry mergers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the D-ETG population has a high incidence of star formation (both in terms of the fraction of galaxies with star formation, and in terms of the star formation rate), a high incidence of active galactic nuclei, a high incidence of merger activity, and an unusually large amount of dust and associated gas.
D-ETGs are a class of galaxies with a high incidence of recent star formation, nuclear activity and merger-induced gas accretion.
the D-ETG population is dominated by gas-rich mergers, with a large fraction of the dust residing in the diffuse interstellar medium, and a small fraction in the clumpy large-scale dust features.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a substantial fraction of the molecular gas in the D-ETG sample was acquired via the merger process, and that the gas accretion rate is likely to have been much greater than the gas consumption rate, at least during the first ∼100 Myr following the merger.
D-ETGs are a diverse population, which is likely to include both gas-poor and gas-rich ETGs.
